cards.title: Types, mutability and truthiness
cards.simple: In Python, every value is like a sealed envelope or a whiteboard. A number or a word is an envelope: you cannot change what is inside, you can only swap in a new envelope. A list is a whiteboard: you can rub things out and write more, and everyone who points at that whiteboard sees the change. Python also treats 'nothing' (empty, zero, None) as 'no' in an if, and everything else as 'yes'. In exam words: lists, dicts and sets are mutable, ints, strs and tuples are immutable, and empty containers, 0 and None are falsy.
cards.idea: Every Python value is an object, and some objects can be changed in place while others cannot. Lists, dicts and sets are mutable: you can change them after they are made. Ints, strings and tuples are immutable: any 'change' builds a new object and moves the name to it. Separately, an if treats empty things, zero and None as False, and almost everything else as True.
cards.definition:
**Mutable:** list, dict, set.

**Immutable:** int, float, bool, str, tuple, frozenset, None.

On an immutable object, `x += 1` or `s += 'a'` builds a new object and rebinds the name. Item assignment such as `t[0] = 1` on a tuple or a string raises TypeError.

**Falsy values:** 0, 0.0, '', [], (), {}, set(), None and False. Everything else is truthy. `bool(x)` shows the verdict. `a or b` and `a and b` return one of their operands, not just True or False.
cards.intuition_full: A Python name is a label, and the label points at an object. Immutable objects, such as numbers and strings, never change after they are created. When you write x += 1, there is no way to alter the 5, so Python makes a 6 and moves the label. Mutable objects, such as lists, can be changed while the label stays where it is. That one difference decides whether other labels pointing at the same object notice a change. For truthiness, think of the question 'is there anything here?'. Zero, empty text and empty containers say no. A container holding something, even a zero or another empty list, says yes. The operators or and and use the same test, and they hand back the operand that settled the answer.

example.setup:
What does this program print?

```python
x = 5
y = x
x += 1
L = [1, 2]
M = L
L += [3]
print(x, y, L, M, bool([]), bool(0.0), bool('0'))
```
steps: x = 5, then y = x. Both names point at the same int object 5.
x += 1 cannot change the object 5. Python builds a new object 6 and moves the name x to it. y still points at 5.
L = [1, 2] and M = L: two names, one list object.
L += [3] changes the list in place, so M sees [1, 2, 3] too.
Truth tests: [] is empty, so False. 0.0 is zero, so False. The string '0' is not empty, so it is True.

cards.why: Mutability explains why some Python programs surprise you. In GATE: you trace a few lines and must know whether a name was rebound to a new object or the same object was changed.
how: Classify each object as mutable or immutable.
For an immutable object, an update rebinds the name to a new object.
For a mutable object, an update changes it in place, and all names see it.
For a condition, empty containers, 0 and None are falsy.
cards.mistake: Expecting a tuple to accept item assignment, or a string method to change the string. Tuples and strings are immutable, so t[0] = 1 raises TypeError. Methods such as s.upper() return a new string.
edge_cases: A one-item tuple needs a comma: (5,) is a tuple and (5) is just 5.
A tuple that contains a list is still changeable through that list.
== compares values and `is` compares identity. Do not use `is` for numbers or strings.
Dict keys must be immutable, so a list cannot be a key.
connections: Aliasing is a consequence of mutability (see Aliasing and copying).
Dict keys and set items must be immutable (see Dictionaries and Sets).
In C, assignment copies a value. In Python it binds a name to an object (see C, Pointers).

cards.title: Lists and slicing
cards.simple: A list is a row of numbered boxes. Counting from the left, the first box is 0. Counting from the right, the last box is -1. A slice is like taking a photo of part of the row: you say where to start and where to stop (the stop box is not in the photo), and you get a copy while the original row stays as it was. A third number means 'skip by this many', and a minus sign means 'walk backwards'. In exam words: s[a:b:c] includes a, excludes b, steps by c, and builds a new list.
cards.idea: A list is a row of numbered cells. Counting from the left starts at 0, and counting from the right starts at -1. A slice s[a:b] copies the cells from index a up to, but not including, index b into a new list. Leave a or b out to mean 'from the start' or 'to the end', and add a third number to take every c-th cell.
cards.definition:
$$s[a:b:c]\ \text{takes indexes } a,\ a+c,\ a+2c,\ \dots \text{ before } b$$

The start a is included and the stop b is excluded. A negative index -k means len(s) - k. A negative step c walks backward. A slice builds a new list and never changes s. Slice ends outside the list are clipped silently, but s[i] with i out of range raises IndexError. Slice assignment `s[a:b] = other` replaces those cells in place, and `del s[a:b]` removes them.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the indexes as marks between the cells, not as the cells themselves. The mark before the first cell is 0 and the mark after the last cell is n. A slice s[a:b] is everything between mark a and mark b. That is why the length is b - a and why a slice never goes wrong when an end is too large: it just stops at the last mark. Negative numbers count the marks from the right end. A step number then says how far to jump between the cells you collect. A negative step flips the direction, and then the defaults flip too: you start at the right end and stop at the left end. Since every slice is a fresh copy, changing the result never changes the original list.

example.setup:
What does this program print?

```python
s = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
print(s[1:4], s[:2], s[-2:], s[::2], s[::-1])
```
steps: Every cell has two indexes: 0 to 5 from the left and -6 to -1 from the right. A slice never changes the list. It builds a new one.
s[1:4] starts at index 1 and stops before index 4. The start cell is included and the stop cell is not: 20, 30, 40.
s[:2] means start at the beginning. The window is the first two cells: 10, 20.
s[-2:] counts from the right. -2 is the same cell as index 4, and with no stop it runs to the end: 50, 60.
s[::2] takes every second cell: indexes 0, 2, 4, which are 10, 30, 50.
s[::-1] walks right to left, so the result is reversed. The original s is untouched.

examples.setup:
With a negative step, the stop is still excluded and the ends are clipped. What is printed?

```python

print(s[4:1:-1], s[-1:-4:-1], s[8:] == '', s[2:100])
```
steps: s = 'GATE2027' has indexes 0 to 7: G A T E 2 0 2 7.
s[4:1:-1] starts at index 4 and walks back, stopping before index 1: indexes 4, 3, 2 give '2', 'E', 'T'.
s[-1:-4:-1] starts at the last cell and stops before index -4 (index 4): indexes 7, 6, 5 give '7', '2', '0'.
s[8:] starts past the end, so it is empty. s[2:100] is clipped to the end: 'TE2027'.
examples.answer: It prints `2ET 720 True TE2027`. A slice never raises an error for an out-of-range end, and a reversed slice excludes its stop cell as well.

cards.why: Slicing is a favourite for short output questions, and one off-by-one decides the answer. In GATE: you read a slice, a reversed slice, or the list after a slice assignment or del.
how: Write the indexes 0 to n-1 under the list.
Start is included and stop is excluded.
The step c skips cells, and a negative step walks backward.
For a slice assignment or del, rewrite the list, then read it.
cards.mistake: Including the stop cell. s[1:4] has 3 cells, not 4. The number of cells in s[a:b] is b - a (if inside the list).
edge_cases: s[2:100] is fine, but s[100] raises IndexError.
A step of 0 raises ValueError.
s[a:b] with a at least b (and a positive step) is empty.
With step -1, the default start is the last cell and the default stop is before the first cell.
connections: Strings slice by the same rules (see Strings and methods).
A slice is a shallow copy (see Aliasing and copying).
In C, the same idea is pointer arithmetic (see C, Arrays and pointer arithmetic).

cards.title: Strings and methods
cards.simple: A word in Python is like a printed ticket. You can read it, copy bits of it and cut it up, but you cannot rub out a letter. Methods such as upper() or replace() do not edit the ticket. They hand you a new ticket. split cuts a sentence into a list of words at a character you choose, and join does the opposite and glues the words back with a glue you choose. In exam words: strings are immutable, methods return new values, split gives a list and sep.join(list) gives a string.
cards.idea: A string is an immutable row of characters, indexed and sliced just like a list. Its methods never change it. They return a new string or a list, so you must use the result. split cuts a string into a list at a separator, and join glues a list of strings back together.
cards.definition: `s.split(sep)` returns the pieces between separators. With no argument it splits on runs of whitespace and drops empty pieces. `sep.join(list)` returns one string with sep between the items. Others: `upper()`, `lower()`, `strip()`, `replace(a, b[, n])`, `find(x)` (an index, or -1 if absent), `count(x)`, `startswith(x)`. All of them return new values. `len(s)` counts characters. `x in s` tests for a substring.
cards.intuition_full: Strings are sequences, so everything you know about indexing and slicing applies. What makes them different from lists is that they are frozen. A line like s.upper() therefore has no visible effect on s, which is a classic exam trap: the new value was computed and thrown away. The two methods that move between strings and lists are the ones to know well. split chooses where to cut. With an explicit separator, every occurrence cuts, so neighbours leave empty pieces. With no argument it cuts on any whitespace and ignores the gaps. join is the exact opposite: the separator goes between items, never at the ends, and the items must already be strings.

example.setup:
What does this program print?

```python
s = 'red;green;;blue'
parts = s.split(';')
print(parts, len(parts), '-'.join(parts), s.upper())
```
steps: split(';') cuts the string at every semicolon. Two semicolons in a row leave an empty string between them.
parts has 4 items: 'red', 'green', an empty string and 'blue'. So len(parts) is 4.
'-'.join(parts) puts a dash between the items. The empty item still gets its dashes: red-green--blue.
s.upper() returns a new string. The original s is unchanged because strings are immutable.

```python
w = t.split()
```

t.find('and'): the characters before it are 'the cat ', which is 8 characters. So the index is 8.

examples.setup:
A method result must be used. What is printed?

```python

s.upper()
t = s.upper()
print(s, t, 'AB' in t, 'ab' in t)
```
steps: s.upper() on its own line builds 'ABC' and throws it away. s is still 'abc'.
t = s.upper() keeps the new string: t is 'ABC'.
'AB' in t is True, because 'AB' is a substring of 'ABC'. 'ab' in t is False, because case matters.
examples.answer: It prints `abc ABC True False`. Strings are immutable, so a method that looks like an update only returns a new value.

For join, put the separator between items only.
cards.mistake: Expecting a method to change the string, as in s.upper() on its own line. Strings are immutable, so the original is unchanged. Use t = s.upper().

''.split(',') is [''] (one empty string), while ''.split() is [].
find returns -1 when absent. index raises ValueError.
'a' in 'abc' tests for a substring, and 'ab' in 'cabd' is True.

cards.title: Aliasing and copying
cards.simple: A name in Python is a sticky label, and objects are the things the labels are stuck on. Writing b = a does not make a second object, it just sticks a second label on the same one. So if you change the object through one label, anyone looking through the other label sees the change. A slice copy a[:] builds a new object, but if the objects inside are lists, those inner objects are still shared, like photocopying a folder but not its attached files. In exam words: assignment binds names and never copies, a[:] is a shallow copy, and copy.deepcopy copies the inner objects too.
cards.idea: Assignment never copies an object in Python. b = a puts a second label on the same object, so a change through one name shows through the other. a[:] builds a new outer list but the items inside are still shared. Only a deep copy copies the items too.
cards.definition:
`b = a` binds a second name to the same object. `b is a` is True.

`a[:]`, `a.copy()` and `list(a)` build a new outer list that holds the same inner objects: a **shallow copy**. `copy.deepcopy(a)` copies the inner objects too.

Changing a mutable object in place (`append`, `+=` on a list, item assignment) is seen through every name. Rebinding a name (`a = a + [3]`) moves only that name.
cards.intuition_full: Python separates names from objects. Assignment only creates or moves a name. That one fact explains everything on this card. cards.title: Dictionaries
cards.simple: A dictionary is like the contact list on your phone. You do not ask for 'the fifth person'. You ask for a name and it gives you that person's number. Each name appears once, and if you add the same name again you replace the number. If the name is not in the list, asking directly gives an error, but asking with .get gives an answer of your choice. This makes counting easy: for each thing you read, look up its count (or 0 if it is new) and add one. In exam words: d[k] raises KeyError, d.get(k, default) does not, and counting uses d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1.
cards.idea: A dictionary stores pairs: a key and the value filed under it, like a phone book. You look a value up by its key, not by position. d[k] gives the value, or raises KeyError if k is missing. d.get(k, default) gives the default instead. A classic use is counting: d[w] = d.get(w, 0) + 1.
cards.definition: `d = {k1: v1, k2: v2}`. `d[k]` reads. `d[k] = v` adds a new key or replaces the value of an existing one, which keeps its place. `k in d` tests keys. Looping over d, `list(d)` and `d.keys()` give the keys in the order they were first inserted. `d.values()` and `d.items()` give the values and the (key, value) pairs. `len(d)` is the number of keys. Keys must be immutable: ints, strings and tuples work, lists do not.
cards.intuition_full: A dict answers one question very quickly: what is filed under this key? It does this by turning the key into a number and jumping to that spot, which is why keys must be immutable. A key that could change after filing would be lost. Every key appears at most once, so writing to an existing key replaces its value in place. The counting idiom builds on that: get returns the old count, or 0 for a first sighting, and the assignment writes the new count back. Since Python 3.7 a dict also remembers the order in which keys were first inserted, so looping gives a predictable order. Updating a value does not change the key's position, but deleting and re-adding does.

```python
d = {}
for ch in word:
    d[ch] = d.get(ch, 0) + 1
print(d, len(d), d.get('z', 0), 'n' in d)
```
steps: d starts empty. For each letter, d.get(ch, 0) gives the current count, or 0 if the letter is new.
b is new, so d['b'] = 0 + 1 = 1. a is new, so d['a'] = 1. n is new, so d['n'] = 1.
a again: d['a'] = 1 + 1 = 2. n again: d['n'] = 2. a again: d['a'] = 3.
Final d = {'b': 1, 'a': 3, 'n': 2}. len(d) is 3. d.get('z', 0) is 0 because z is absent, and 'n' in d is True.

cards.title: Sets
cards.simple: A set is a bag of unique tokens. Put the same token in again and nothing changes, and the tokens have no order. With two bags you can ask four questions: which tokens are in both, which are in either, which are only in the first bag, and which are in just one of them. Python has a symbol for each: & for both, | for either, - for only the first and ^ for exactly one. In exam words: sets drop duplicates and have no order, and & | - ^ are intersection, union, difference and symmetric difference.
cards.idea: A set is a bag where each item appears at most once and the order does not matter. Putting the same item in twice changes nothing. Sets answer 'is it in there?' quickly and combine groups with four operators: & keeps what is in both, | keeps what is in either, - keeps what is only in the first, ^ keeps what is in exactly one.
cards.definition: A set literal is `{1, 2, 3}`. The empty set is `set()`, because `{}` is an empty dict. Operators: `A & B` intersection, `A | B` union, `A - B` difference, `A ^ B` symmetric difference. Methods: `add`, `remove` (KeyError if absent), `discard` (no error), `update`. `x in A` is fast. `len(A)` counts distinct items. Elements must be immutable. The printing order of a set is not reliable, so sort before printing.
cards.intuition_full: A set keeps one copy of each distinct item and forgets the order they arrived in. That makes membership tests cheap and removes duplicates for free. The four operators are the Venn diagram of two circles. Intersection is the overlap. Union is both circles together. Difference is one circle with the overlap cut out, which is why it depends on which circle you start from. Symmetric difference is everything except the overlap, so it is the union minus the intersection. In loops that build a set, the common pattern is 'have I seen this before?': test with in, then add. If you need an answer in a fixed order, sort, because a printed set may come out in any order.

steps: A = {2, 4, 6, 8} and B = {4, 8, 9}. The items 4 and 8 are in both.
A & B keeps the items in both: {4, 8}.
A | B keeps the items in either, each listed once: {2, 4, 6, 8, 9}.
A - B keeps the items of A that are not in B: {2, 6}.
A ^ B keeps the items in exactly one of the two: {2, 6, 9}. That is (A | B) minus (A & B).

cards.title: Comprehensions
cards.simple: A list comprehension is a shortcut for a loop that fills a list. Imagine a canteen queue: you walk down the line, you only let in students who have a ticket, and for each one you write down their roll number doubled. The one-line version says the same three things: what to write down, who to look at, and which ones to allow. To read one, unfold it into an ordinary for loop with an if inside. In exam words: [expr for x in it if cond] loops over it, filters with the if, and collects expr.
cards.idea: A list comprehension is a loop that builds a list in one line. [x * x for x in nums if x > 0] means: go through nums, keep the items that pass the if, and for each one collect x * x. To read one, unfold it back into a for loop with the if inside. Nested ones read like nested loops, outermost first.
cards.definition:
`[expr for x in it if cond]` is the same as:

```python
result = []
for x in it:
    if cond:
        result.append(expr)
```

The if is optional and filters before expr is computed. With two for clauses, `[e for a in A for b in B]`, the first for is the outer loop. A conditional value `x if c else y` placed before the for is part of expr. The set form `{e for ...}` removes duplicates. A generator expression `(e for ...)` makes the items one at a time.
cards.intuition_full: A comprehension is a for loop with the body moved to the front. The reading order is the loop order: first the for clauses, left to right, outermost first, then the if, and only then the expression is evaluated for what survived. That is why unfolding is a reliable method. Write the for lines one under another, indent each deeper, put the if inside, and put the append of expr at the bottom. The one thing that trips people is the position of an if-else. When the if comes after the for, it is a filter and the else is not allowed. When an if-else comes before the for, it is part of the expression, so every item produces a value.

cards.title: Iteration tools and sorting
cards.simple: zip is the zipper on a jacket. It joins the left row and the right row tooth by tooth, and it stops when the shorter side runs out. enumerate hands you a numbered list, like giving each student a roll number as they walk past. sorted puts things in order and gives you a new list, leaving the original alone. If two things tie, a stable sort keeps them in the order they came, like students of the same height staying in their queue order. In exam words: zip stops at the shorter input, enumerate counts from start, and sorted with key= is stable and returns a new list.
cards.idea: A few built-ins pair up or order your data. zip walks two lists side by side and stops when the shorter one ends. enumerate adds a counter. sorted returns a new list in order, and its key says what to sort by. Sorting is stable: items that tie keep the order they came in.
cards.definition: `zip(a, b)` yields pairs (a[i], b[i]) and stops at the shorter input. `enumerate(it, start)` yields (start + i, item) pairs, and start defaults to 0. `sorted(it, key=f, reverse=False)` returns a new sorted list, ordered by f(item). `L.sort()` sorts in place and returns None. **Stable** means items with equal keys keep their input order. This holds even with reverse=True. Tuples compare item by item, so `key=lambda p: (p[1], p[0])` sorts by the second item, then the first.
cards.intuition_full: These helpers all work on the idea of an iterable, anything you can loop over once. zip and enumerate do not build lists, they make a stream of tuples as you ask for it, which is why you wrap them in list() to see them. sorted is different: it must see all the items, so it builds a new list. The key function is called once per item, and the items are ordered by those keys. Stability is a promise about ties: two items with the same key stay in their original relative order. That promise is what makes multi-level sorting work, and it holds even if you ask for reverse order. A tuple key such as (-len, word) is the standard way to sort by one thing and break ties by another.

```python
ages = [30, 25, 30]
print(list(zip(names, ages)), list(enumerate(names, 1))[1], sorted(names, key=len), sorted(names, reverse=True))
```
steps: zip pairs the lists by position and stops when the shorter list ends. names has 4 items and ages has 3, so there are 3 pairs and 'di' is dropped.
enumerate(names, 1) counts from 1: (1, 'bo'), (2, 'al'), (3, 'cy'), (4, 'di'). Index 1 of that list is (2, 'al').
sorted(names, key=len): every name has length 2, so all keys tie. A stable sort keeps the input order.
sorted(names, reverse=True) sorts by dictionary order, largest first: di, cy, bo, al.

cards.title: Functions and scope
cards.simple: A function is like a recipe card. The default amounts on the card are written once, when you write the card, not each time you cook. If a default is an empty bowl and each cook keeps adding to that same bowl, the next cook finds the old ingredients still in it. That is the famous default-list surprise. A function inside a function also looks up names when it runs, not when it was written, so it sees the latest value. In exam words: defaults are evaluated once at def time, and closures look up variables at call time.
cards.idea: A default value is written on the function once, when the def line runs, not every time you call it. If the default is a list and the function changes it, the next call finds the old contents still there. In the same way, a function defined inside another one looks up names when it runs, not when it was written, so it sees the latest value.
cards.definition:
A default argument is evaluated once, when `def` runs, and the object is stored with the function. A mutable default is therefore shared by all calls that do not pass their own. The safe pattern is `L=None` and `if L is None: L = []` inside the body.

A name used inside a function is looked up when the function runs: first in the function, then in enclosing functions, then at module level. A closure sees the current value of the enclosing variable, not the value at definition time. Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local to the whole function. `global x` lets the function rebind the module's x, and `nonlocal x` rebinds an enclosing function's x.
cards.intuition_full: Two moments matter in Python: when def runs, and when the function is called. Everything in the def line, including default values, is evaluated at the first moment and kept. The body is only run at the second moment, and every name in it is looked up then. That single timeline explains both traps. A default list is created at the first moment and reused by every call, so changes pile up. A closure looks up its outer variable at the second moment, so it reflects whatever value that variable has by then, including a change made after the inner function was defined. To avoid the default trap, use None as a signal and build the real list inside the body, which runs fresh on every call.

example.setup:
What does this program print, and how is it fixed?

```python
def add(x, L=[]):
    L.append(x)
    return L
print(add(1))
print(add(2))
```
steps: When Python runs the def line, it builds the default [] once and keeps it with the function. It is not rebuilt for each call.
add(1) uses the default, so L is that same list. It appends 1 and returns [1].
add(2) gets the same default list, which already holds 1. The result is [1, 2], not [2].
Fix: default to None and build the list inside the body. Then every call gets a fresh list, and add(2) returns [2].

```python
    if L is None:

    L.append(x)
    return L
print(add(1))
print(add(2))
```

it prints `[1]` and then `[2]`.

cards.title: Generators and iterators
cards.simple: A generator is like a vending machine that gives you one snack each time you press the button, then waits. It remembers exactly where it was, so the next press gives the next snack. It never hands out the same snack twice, and when the machine is empty it stays empty: pressing the button again gets you nothing. You cannot refill it, but you can get a brand-new machine by calling the function again. In exam words: yield pauses the function and keeps its locals, next() resumes it, and a finished generator is empty.
cards.idea: A generator is a function that can pause. Instead of return, it uses yield to hand back one value and freeze with all its local variables. The next call to next() wakes it up exactly where it stopped. When it runs out, it is finished, and it stays empty: you cannot rewind it.
cards.definition: A function that contains `yield` returns a generator object when called, and no code runs yet. `next(g)` runs until the next yield and returns the yielded value. When the function ends, next raises StopIteration. `list(g)`, `sum(g)` and a for loop use the generator up. A used-up generator gives nothing more. A generator expression `(x * x for x in it)` behaves the same way. Calling the function again makes a brand-new generator.
cards.intuition_full: A normal function runs to the end and throws its locals away. A generator function is different: yield is a pause button. The function hands back one value, and its whole state, including the line it is on and every local variable, is kept. The next request resumes from that exact line. This is why a generator can describe a long or even endless sequence using a few variables. It also explains the one-shot behaviour. The progress through the function is part of the state, and there is no instruction to go back. Once the function has run off its end, the generator is finished. Anything that consumes it, such as list, sum or a for loop, moves it forward, so a second consumer finds only what is left.

example.setup:
What does this program print?

```python
def count(n):
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        yield i * 10
        i += 1
g = count(3)
print(next(g), next(g), list(g), list(g))
```
steps: count(3) runs no code yet. It returns a generator g that is waiting at the start.
next(g) runs until the first yield. i is 0, so it yields 0 and freezes there with i = 0.
next(g) wakes up after the yield, runs i += 1, loops, and yields 10. It freezes with i = 1.
list(g) takes the rest: it wakes up, yields 20, then i becomes 3, the while loop ends and the function ends. The result is [20].
The generator is used up. A second list(g) finds nothing: [] .

cards.what: A generator is a function that can pause. Instead of return, it uses yield to hand back one value and freeze with all its local variables. The next call to next() wakes it up exactly where it stopped. When it runs out, it is finished, and it stays empty: you cannot rewind it.
cards.what_full:
A generator is a function that can pause. Instead of return, it uses yield to hand back one value and freeze with all its local variables. The next call to next() wakes it up exactly where it stopped. When it runs out, it is finished, and it stays empty: you cannot rewind it.

A function that contains `yield` returns a generator object when called, and no code runs yet. `next(g)` runs until the next yield and returns the yielded value. When the function ends, next raises StopIteration. `list(g)`, `sum(g)` and a for loop use the generator up. A used-up generator gives nothing more. A generator expression `(x * x for x in it)` behaves the same way. Calling the function again makes a brand-new generator.

**Worked example.** What does this program print?

```python
def count(n):
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        yield i * 10
        i += 1
g = count(3)
print(next(g), next(g), list(g), list(g))
```

1. count(3) runs no code yet. It returns a generator g that is waiting at the start.
2. next(g) runs until the first yield. i is 0, so it yields 0 and freezes there with i = 0.
3. next(g) wakes up after the yield, runs i += 1, loops, and yields 10. It freezes with i = 1.
4. list(g) takes the rest: it wakes up, yields 20, then i becomes 3, the while loop ends and the function ends. The result is [20].
5. The generator is used up. A second list(g) finds nothing: [] .

**Answer:** It prints `0 10 [20] []`.

cards.title: Recursion in Python
cards.simple: Recursion is like a set of Russian dolls. To find the biggest doll you open the outer one and ask the smaller doll the same question, and so on until you reach the tiniest doll, which needs no more opening. Then the answers pass back up, each doll comparing its own size with what it was told. In Python you often 'open a doll' by taking L[0] as the item and L[1:] as the smaller list. In exam words: each call has its own variables, the base case stops the chain, and the answers are combined as the calls return.
cards.idea: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input until it reaches a base case that needs no further call. Python lists make this easy: L[0] is the first item and L[1:] is the rest. Every call has its own local variables, and the calls wait in a pile until the base case answers and the answers flow back up.
cards.intuition_full: Recursion trusts a simple idea: if I can solve a slightly smaller version, I can finish the job. For a list, 'smaller' usually means the list without its first item. The base case is the version so small that the answer is obvious, such as an empty list or one item. When you trace, the calls form a stack. Each call waits at the line where it called itself, with its own copy of L and any local variables. Nothing is returned until the base case answers. Then the answers come back one at a time, each call using the value it was waiting for. Two cautions come from Python itself. L[1:] makes a copy every time, and there is a depth limit.

```python
    m = big(L[1:])

print(big([4, 9, 2, 7]))
```

big([2, 7]) gets m = 7. Is 2 > 7? No, so it returns m = 7.
big([9, 2, 7]) gets m = 7. Is 9 > 7? Yes, so it returns 9.

cards.title: Numeric semantics
cards.simple: Python's whole-number division always rounds down to the next smaller number, like stepping down a staircase. So -7 divided by 2 is -3.5, and going down gives -4. The leftover is whatever makes the sum work again, and it takes the sign of the number you divide by. The power sign works from the right, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 means 2 to the power 9. And plain / always gives a decimal answer. In exam words: // floors, % takes the sign of the divisor, ** is right-associative, and / returns a float.
cards.idea: Python's whole-number division rounds down, not toward zero. So -7 // 2 is -4, and the remainder -7 % 2 is 1, which takes the sign of the divisor. The two always fit together: (a // b) * b + a % b gives back a. The power operator ** works from the right, and / always gives a decimal.
cards.definition:
$$a = (a\,//\,b)\cdot b + a\,\%\,b$$

a // b is the floor of the exact quotient. a % b has the sign of b. `a ** b ** c` means `a ** (b ** c)`. a / b is always a float, so 6 / 3 is 2.0. For floats, 7.5 // 2 is 3.0. `divmod(a, b)` gives the pair (a // b, a % b). `round()` sends halves to the nearest even number: round(2.5) is 2. Ints never overflow.
cards.intuition_full: Python makes one choice and keeps everything else consistent with it: integer division rounds toward minus infinity. Given that, the remainder is forced. It must be whatever restores a = (a // b) * b + a % b, and a quick check shows that this remainder has the sign of the divisor. C picks the other choice, rounding toward zero, so its remainder follows the dividend. That is why the same numbers give different answers in the two languages. The power operator is also unusual: unlike + and *, which group from the left, ** groups from the right, so a ** b ** c is a to the power (b to the power c). Finally, / is true division and always returns a float, even when the result is whole.

chapter_note.simple: Python hides its memory, but the one thing you must picture is that names are labels stuck on objects. A number or a word is a sealed envelope that never changes, and a list is a whiteboard that anyone holding a label can rewrite. Most exam questions give you a few lines and ask what is printed, so you track which labels point at which objects, and what each line really does. A few special rules decide the tricky ones: copying a list copies only the outer layer, a default value is made once, a generator can be used only once, and whole-number division rounds down.
